arrivals.title: Sound familiar?
arrivals.sub: Four ways a credential reaches you. One answer, whichever it was.
arrivals.thesis: However it arrives, the contract is the same: one verdict, one receipt, one rule you wrote.
arrivals.requirementsNote: Three states, never two. What could not be checked is said, not assumed.

items.quote: They send you a PDF and an AI could have made it.
items.arrivalNote: PDF or image, straight from the candidate
items.answer: We read the credential sealed inside the file, or the code that points at it. If it carries nothing signed, we say so instead of guessing.

items.quote: The issuer never answers the phone.
items.arrivalNote: issued somewhere else, handed to you
items.answer: We resolve the issuer's own identity and check their signature against it. Nobody has to pick up.

items.quote: It lives on the candidate's phone.
items.arrivalNote: the holder chooses what to show
items.answer: They present it, they choose which fields to reveal, and you get the same verdict as every other way in.

items.quote: It only exists inside a portal you do not control.
items.arrivalNote: no integration on the issuer's side
items.answer: We read it where it lives and turn it into the same signed evidence, without asking the issuer for anything.

dev.title: For developers, it is one call
dev.body: A REST API that behaves. Verify a credential you did not issue, get a verdict you can act on, and keep the signed receipt that proves what you checked.
dev.responseNote: Product preview: the API you'll integrate.

items.a: Credentials issued through Glemo, and credentials issued elsewhere that arrive as a portable file: we resolve the issuer's own DID and check their signature, their schema and their status list. Certificate images too, when the file carries a signed credential inside or a QR that points at one.

items.q: Do I have to trust your criteria?
items.a: No, and that is the whole point. You write the rule: which credential types you accept, from which issuers, which fields have to be there. Two companies can reach opposite conclusions about the same credential and both be right.

items.q: What do I get to keep?
items.a: A signed receipt for every check, whatever the outcome. It is a Security Event Token, so any JWT library verifies it against our public keys without calling us. We keep no copy, so if you need it later, save it.
Your credentials keep working and your receipts keep verifying. Everything sits on open standards and can be exported. We think that is the only honest way to build this.

items.q: Do recipients need a wallet or an account?
items.a: No. A credential is a link. They open it, share it and that is the whole experience: no wallet, no password, no app to install.

Issuing credentials is free. Verifiers pay per verification: every plan includes a monthly allowance and publishes the rate that applies after it. Design partners get generous early terms, that could be you.

pricing.title: Pricing
pricing.subtitle: Verifiers pay for verifications. Issuing credentials is always free. No wallet, no per-seat fees, no lock-in.
pricing.featureCore: Verification by ID, link or credential file
pricing.featureZkTls: Verify credentials from a supported portal (zkTLS) — Sandbox
pricing.footnote: Every plan includes the independent trust mark, the public verification page and the full API. Overage on paid plans is billed monthly at the per-verification rate above.

faq.a1: One verification transaction: a call to the API, or one verification session opened against a rule and answered. It counts once whatever the outcome, because verifying and finding a credential revoked is the work you asked for. Issuing credentials never counts. Checking the same credential again is a new transaction and counts again, in the same period or any other.
faq.q2: What happens when I pass my included verifications?
faq.a2: On Free, verification is capped: further calls are blocked until the next period, so you are never charged by surprise. On Starter and Scale, extra verifications are billed monthly at the per-verification rate on the plan.
faq.a3: Yes. Anyone can issue credentials, design templates and share the public credential page at no cost. Only the verifier side, the relying parties consuming the API, pays.
faq.q4: Do my recipients need a wallet or an account?
faq.a4: No. A credential is a link. Recipients open it and share it without installing anything, and verifiers confirm it with one API call.
faq.a5: Any time, from your workspace. Upgrades apply immediately; the included quota and the per-verification rate change with the plan.

accessibility.noticeBody: Every figure below comes from a check that runs on each change, and the limits section names what those checks cannot see. This is not a claim of full conformity.
accessibility.title: Accessibility statement
accessibility.intro: Glemo is committed to making its verification network usable by everyone, including people who navigate with a keyboard, a screen reader, or a magnified screen. This statement says what we measure, what the measurements show, and what they do not cover.
accessibility.standardTitle: The standard we hold ourselves to
accessibility.standardBody: EN 301 549, the European harmonised standard, which references WCAG 2.1 at level AA. It is the standard the European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882, applicable since 28 June 2025) points to for digital services.
accessibility.stateBody: Every claim below is produced by a check that runs on every change, not by a one-off review. The figures are the ones those checks last reported.
accessibility.stateAxe: Automated auditing with axe-core on the WCAG 2.1 A and AA rule sets, across the sign-in pages, the application, the issuer surfaces, the administration console and the public credential page, including a deliberately hostile issuer brand colour: zero violations of serious or critical impact.
accessibility.stateLighthouse: Lighthouse scores the accessibility category at 1.0 on the sign-in, sign-up and password-reset pages, and the build fails below 0.95.
accessibility.stateContrast: Colour contrast is a test, not an opinion: eleven declared foreground and background pairs are computed and checked against their WCAG ratio, 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for large text and icons. The lowest passing pair sits at 4.80.
accessibility.stateResponsive: Layouts are verified at 1440 and 390 pixels wide with no horizontal scrolling, so a magnified screen does not push content out of reach.
accessibility.stateMotion: Motion respects the operating system's reduced-motion setting, verified end to end rather than declared.
accessibility.limitsBody: Automated tools find a minority of accessibility barriers. Naming the gaps is part of the statement, not an appendix to it.
accessibility.limitsAssistive: We have not conducted an audit with assistive technology users. No screen reader walkthrough, no keyboard-only usability session, and no review by a person with a disability has been performed. This is the most significant gap, and automated coverage does not substitute for it.
accessibility.limitsLighthouseScope: Lighthouse runs against the three pages that need no account. The signed-in application is covered by axe and by the responsive checks, but not by Lighthouse.
accessibility.limitsLanguage: The application is available in English and Spanish. The developer documentation, the legal pages and the service status page are currently English only.
accessibility.limitsThirdParty: The sign-in page embeds Google's sign-in button, which we do not control and which is the reason our best-practices score sits at 0.96 rather than 1.0.
accessibility.limitsIssuerContent: Issuers choose the wording, images and brand colours on the credentials they design. We check that our own components and palettes meet contrast requirements; we cannot guarantee the content an issuer writes.
accessibility.methodBody: The checks above run in continuous integration on every change and block the build when they fail. They are not a snapshot: a regression turns the build red before it reaches anyone.
accessibility.reviewedBody: 4 September 2026. This statement is reviewed whenever the checks it describes change, and at least once a year.
accessibility.contactBody: If something here is not usable for you, write to hello@glemo.io and describe what you were trying to do. We answer within five working days. If our answer does not resolve it, you can escalate to the enforcement body for the European Accessibility Act in your country.
